newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saudi barley purchase fails to ignite EU tender.
newsitem.headline: Saudi barley purchase fails to ignite EU tender.

text.p: Grain firms chose to play safe on Thursday by not rushing to bid for barley from the European Union to cover the latest sale to Saudi Arabia, traders said.
A weekly export tender attracted bids for a quarter of a million of tonnes of barley compared with the 600,000 to 800,000 tonnes the EU expects to supply to Riyadh, they said.
Saudi Arabia bought 1.2 million tonnes of optional-origin barley for February and March delivery on Wednesday.
Those bids which arrived on Thursday seemed mostly to be for other business, traders said.
"There is time to spare, there is no need to hurry," said one trader, adding that as usual traders and the European Commission seemed to disagree over what barley was worth.
Commission sources suggested on Wednesday they were willing to sell barley but only above $140 per tonne on an fob basis.
The best bid through France at Thursday's tender was equivalent to $141 per tonne for January but it only covered 25,000 tonnes, traders said.
Others bids went as low as $136 per tonne, which was more in line with prices quoted for barley of $136 to $138 a tonne.
Iran was reported to have bought at least 100,000 tonnes of optional-origin barley at below $140 per tonne.
Traders bid through France for 246,000 tonnes of free-market EU barley at refunds of 27.98 to 31.82 Ecus per tonne.
Through Germany they sought 34,000 tonnes at refunds of 24.95 to 34.01 Ecus.
The slow start to bidding followed the pattern of recent Saudi barley deals. These have tended to be covered at the last moment after sometimes tense debate between traders and the Commission.
A lack of clarity over the amount of barley likely to qualify for malting in Europe this year was also slowing things down.
Some traders said they doubted the Commission would take a tough stand this time because of its concerns that intervention stocks would pile up again after a large 1996 harvest.
Brussels is paying even more attention than usual to expenditure because of higher than budgeted export refunds and a $1 billion bill for dealing with the mad cow crisis.
Several traders were confident that Brussels would tone down its price demands in coming weeks rather than be out of such a major piece of export business.
"The price is fine as long as they carry the barley to Saudi Arabia themselves," joked one trader, referring to the Commission's price tag of more than $140 per tonne.
Freight to Saudi Arabia is pegged around $20 per tonne.
But with two-thirds of the grain expected to come from Europe, and few if any traders said to be long of licences, the Commission would try to stick to its guns, grain officials said.
Canada was not expected to do much because of weather-related loading delays at Vancouver and the lack of barley in port.
North American traders said on Wednesday that Canada was rumoured to have lined up 200,000 tonnes for March at $138 a tonne fob, and Australia another 200,000 tonnes.
Grain traders in Australia said on Thursday they doubted that country would take a big part of the Saudi purchase, also because of supply tightness, but gave no estimate of volumes.
